Lázaro Cárdenas. The Mexican president from 1934 to 1940 who implemented the social revolution promised by the Constitution of 1917. He distributed millions of acres to peasants, nationalised foreign oil companies, and championed indigenous rights and labour reform.

Cárdenas distributed over forty-nine million acres of land to peasant communities, the largest agrarian reform in Mexican history and the fulfilment of Emiliano Zapata's vision. He exiled former president Plutarco Elías Calles, consolidating executive power and ending the era when strongmen controlled the government from the shadows. In 1938, Cárdenas nationalised the oil industry, seizing foreign-held petroleum assets and establishing the state monopoly PEMEX. He created the ejido system of communal agricultural land, making rural properties collective holdings for peasant communities rather than private estates. He promoted indigenous education and culture, creating schools and supporting indigenous autonomy. His presidency marked the full realisation of revolutionary ideals and the consolidation of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, the PRI, which would dominate Mexican politics for decades. Through these acts, Cárdenas completed the transformation that Zapata had fought for and that Madero's moderate reforms had failed to deliver.
